title: Exponentials and logarithms
summary: Exponential decay loses the same fraction per step; ln undoes exp; log axes turn exponentials into straight lines. Used in absorption (week 1), carrier densities (week 2) and diffusion (week 3).

diagrams.title: Exponential decay, linear and log axis
diagrams.tryThis: Change the decay length and watch where the curve crosses 37 % and 10 %; then switch to a log axis and see the curve become a straight line.

checks.prompt: A material has α = 100 cm⁻¹. How thick (in µm) must a layer be to absorb 90 % of the light in one pass?
hints: ln 10 = 2.303; then convert cm to µm.

checks.prompt: What percentage of the light is left after two penetration depths ($z = 2/\alpha$)?
You plot $y = e^{-x/L}$ with a logarithmic y-axis and a linear x-axis. What does the curve look like?

options.feedback: Correct: $\ln y = -x/L$ is linear in x, and a log axis plots ln y (up to a constant factor).

options.text: A curve that flattens out towards zero
options.feedback: That is what you see on a *linear* y-axis. On a log axis the curve never reaches zero; every equal step in x drops it by the same factor.
No squares are involved: $\ln y = -x/L$ is a straight line.
That would mean y is constant. y keeps falling by a fixed factor per step.

hints: Take the logarithm of both sides.
What kind of graph is ‘something = constant × x’?
solution: On a log y-axis this is a straight line with slope −1/L (per factor e). This is why absorption coefficients and carrier densities are always plotted on log axes.
